Title: Mixed signals on inflation

Summary: 
Inflation in the country has risen to 3.4% by August 2025, up from 3.6% in 2024, and is projected to reach 4% by year-end, prompting the government to implement the Price Stabilisation Fund as a short-term measure. While the fund offers limited relief—impacting at most 10% of CPI weights—it does not address root causes. Wage trends show a significant increase: the Wage Rate Index rose 6.7% from Q4 2022 to 2023 and 14.4% from Q4 2023 to 2024, with manufacturing wages up 54% over three years (Q4 2021–2024), contributing to inflation and reduced competitiveness. However, wage growth is now tapering, supported by a government wage policy in January 2025 that aligns increases with inflation and discourages multiple annual hikes. Additionally, the phasing out of allowances such as housing, child, and maternity benefits has reduced demand, dampening consumption growth from 3.9% in 2024 to a projected 2.9% in real terms in 2025. Import prices, which are highly correlated with inflation, show a downward trend in 2024–2025, especially for petroleum products and certain commodities, though prices for items like meat, dairy, and fresh vegetables remain volatile. The rupee has stabilized, appreciating 1.7% against the dollar between October 2024 and October 2025, which has helped curb inflation, though it depreciated over 6% against the euro. Producer prices are rising: the Manufacturing PPI is expected to grow by over 6% in 2025, double the 2024 increase, and the Agricultural PPI, though volatile, is expected to stabilize. Agricultural output has increased by 29% in the first half of 2025, helping moderate inflation despite earlier spikes in vegetable prices. Indirect taxes, including excise duties on sugary products, have already taken effect and will have a minor inflationary impact. Overall, while some factors like exchange rate stability, declining imports, and agricultural output are moderating inflation, others—wages, producer prices, and indirect taxes—are pressuring it upward. The Price Stabilisation Fund provides psychological relief but is not a sustainable solution. The conclusion emphasizes that consistent policy and bold structural reforms, particularly in domestic production, are essential to long-term inflation control.

Title: Esperan el dólar no rompa el techo de la banda y que la inflación se mantenga por debajo del 2%

Summary: 
According to the Relevamiento de Expectativas de Mercado (REM) of the Banco Central, private economists expect inflation to remain below 2% monthly in the coming months, with the dollar's rise slowing down and the major exchange rate ending the year without breaking the ceiling of $1,460. The REM reflects the projections made between July 29 and 31 by over 40 consultancies and banks. They estimate an inflation rate of 1.8% for July (0.1 percentage points lower than the previous survey). If these estimates are confirmed, the Consumer Price Index for July will be above 1.6% in June, but it will be the third consecutive month with a reading below 2%. In fact, they calculate that in August it will also be 1.8%, and then it will mark 1.7% between September and December, to reach 1.5% in January of next year. For all of 2025, the forecast is 29.5%. 'For the coming months, a general downward trend in inflation projections is expected, with monthly figures always below 2%', details the Central. Regarding the dollar, the consultancies predict a nominal major exchange rate of $1,315 for the average of August 2025, below the current level of $1,330. Even among the top 10 analysts, the projection is $1,304. For December 2025, they see the dollar at $1,405, which would imply a year-over-year expected variation of 37.6%, a level 7.9 percentage points higher than in the REM of June. This implies that despite the rebound of the past week, which took the major to $1,375 and left it just 6% below the ceiling of $1,460, analysts agree that the escalation will slow down. In the July survey, the group of economists estimated that the quarterly GDP adjusted for seasonality between April and June would have grown 0.8% compared to the first quarter of 2025. This implies an improvement of 0.4 percentage points compared to the previous survey. They project that it will decelerate to a growth rate of 0.5% in the third quarter and then expand 0.6% in the fourth. For 2025, they expect an average real GDP level 5% higher than the average of 2024. The open unemployment rate for the second quarter of 2025 was estimated at 7.6%, an increase of 0.2 points compared to the previous REM. As for the rate, after a turbulent July that at times took it above 70%, the forecast is that it will go down in the coming months. Thus, for December, they expect a TAMAR of private banks of 34.85% TNA, equivalent to a monthly effective rate of 2.9%. For December, they project a nominal annual rate of 29.5% (TEM of 2.5%). Regarding foreign trade in goods, they anticipate exports of $81,662 million and imports of $75,115 million for 2025. The estimated annual trade surplus is $6,507 million. Finally, the projection of the primary fiscal result of the Non-Financial Public Sector is a surplus of $13.6 billion for this year. The average of the Top 10 forecast a primary surplus of $14.3 billion.

Published date: August 06 2025, 22:16
